newsitem.title: UK: Politics, economics diverge in EMU rush - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Politics, economics diverge in EMU rush - analysts.

text.p: In the race to be among the founding members of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), some politicians may not realise that their ambitions plans are not in synch with economic reality, analysts said on Friday.
EMU is becoming an electoral issue not only in countries, such as Britain, which are unsure about a single currency in Europe, but also in core supporters such as Germany and France.

Governments face pressure from their electorates and opposition parties by undertaking unpopular economic policies in an effort to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of 1997. "The key thing is that Europe is going through severe, self imposed, synchronised fiscal contraction which is taking a lot of potential growth stimulus out of European economies at a time when they desperately need it," said David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Sterns International in London.
"What Europe needs at this time is faster growth and lower unemployment but we seem to be going in the opposite direction."
He said lacklustre growth of between 1.50 and 1.75 percent was well below the optimum potential and could spark rising unemployment, currently running at an average 11.5 percent across Europe.

"This is obviously not good news for any political party," said Brown. "For an incumbent government it's a huge thorny problem because any opposition party can pick up on it and promote it as a real issue at the next election."
Already in the recent national budgets for 1997, compromises had been made to ensure the budget proposals were passed by parliaments.

"Despite all the talk of governments really biting the bullet in budgets, many, especially those with the largest fiscal problems to solve, haven't done so in a convincing way," said Norman Williams, European economist at BZW in London.
If EMU was not presented and marketed well, there was a risk it would attract a degree of opposition among electorates, he said.

"There is a significant risk that regardless of the merits of the case for or against EMU, it will be blamed for many of the problems that may arise. It will be easy to blame something new and radical," Williams said.
Gareth Crooker, senior researcher at Control Risks Group in London, a political analysis team, cited Britain as an example where both the ruling and oppostion parties were internally split over EMU.
"Although EMU becomes a stick to beat the government with, it doesn't mean to say there won't be supporters as well as opponents within any subsequent government," he said.
Not many centrist oppositions would completely reject EMU, although they might go part of the way down that path to exploit the political situation, Crooker said.
"They will recognise that the national interest may dictate the fact that they are better in than out," he said.
Crooker said the preparation time for EMU was roughly the same as the electoral cycle of many European countries. Many countries were now resigned to this fact.
The French government will want the decision out of the way before parliamentary elections in the April 1998, in order to prevent it from becoming an election issue, analysts said.
Germany too faces elections in 1998 but not until October --in theory after the EMU decision, they said.
Once EMU is established, Brown said the continuing pain for Europe could be massive.
"If (German finance minister Theo) Waigel's vision of a post-EMU stability pact comes on board it means not just one more year of fiscal austerity, it means three to five more years," said Brown.
He said the ultimate objective of the German formula was to squeeze budget deficits down to one percent.

"EMU is going to be a bumpy road to travel down both at a macro and a domestic political level over the next few years," said Brown. "There are 15 different stories in Europe and a whole myriad of problems ahead."
